ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, polished presentation style during formal talks and much briefer, informal exchanges before and after them. Overlap and interruptions are common but generally friendly: people jump in with “yeah,” “right,” or quick follow-ups, and technical questions often develop collaboratively rather than as tightly structured Q&A. The overall register is casual-professional, with frequent greetings, joking, praise, and conversational fillers such as “um,” “you know,” “sort of,” “like,” and repeated starts or self-corrections. Speakers hedge often—“I think,” “maybe,” “it seems,” “we’re interested in,” “I don’t know”—especially when interpreting results or speculating. Challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity (“have you looked at…,” “do you think…,” “what makes…”), while responses validate the question before qualifying the answer. Questions tend to be multi-part, exploratory, and sometimes reformulated mid-sentence; answers are generous, discursive, and acknowledge uncertainty rather than claiming firm conclusions.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.

  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether brain-imaging evidence of awareness in unresponsive patients should count in end-of-life decisions.

speakers.name: Dr. Imani Shah
speakers.background: Dr. Shah is a cognitive neuroscientist with 14 years of experience studying disorders of consciousness in ICU and rehabilitation populations. She oversees EEG motor-imagery paradigms and fMRI command-following protocols, including signal-quality review, preregistered analysis pipelines, replication attempts, and multidisciplinary interpretation of individual patient results. Her work includes distinguishing task noncompliance, arousal fluctuation, motion artifact, and classifier error from evidence consistent with covert command-following.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She treats a positive result as an inference from a constrained experimental paradigm: reproducibility can strengthen evidence that a patient followed a command under specified conditions, but it does not by itself establish the breadth, stability, frequency, or everyday accessibility of awareness. She is especially alert to overinterpretation of single-subject neuroimaging findings and keeps false-negative risk analytically separate from the meaning of a positive result.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Morris
speakers.background: Dr. Morris has 6 years of postdoctoral and clinical-ethics experience focused on consciousness, surrogate decision-making, and end-of-life care. She has consulted on ethics cases involving severe brain injury and has conducted qualitative interviews with families, clinicians, and ethics committee members about how uncertainty is communicated. Her scholarship uses conceptual analysis, normative argument, and case comparison rather than empirical testing alone.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She focuses on the moral bridge between evidence of awareness and claims about what is owed to a patient. For her, wording such as 'interests that must be protected' is not a neutral summary of a scan result: it may invoke different accounts of moral status, welfare, harm, and treatment-relevant interests. She presses the group to distinguish a finding that should enrich deliberation from one that changes what treatments are ethically permissible or required.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Daniel Wu
speakers.background: Dr. Wu is a neurointensivist with 16 years of practice in a tertiary hospital, including attending responsibility for patients with severe traumatic brain injury, stroke, anoxic injury, and prolonged unresponsiveness. He leads family conferences, prognostic consultations, and referrals to the ethics committee, and has helped implement bedside EEG and multimodal neuroprognostication pathways. He is accustomed to documenting uncertainty while helping families understand what decisions remain theirs to make.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He evaluates proposed wording by asking how it will function during an ICU family meeting and an ethics consultation. He can see at least two operational readings of a statement about protected interests: one could require clinicians to treat any credible sign of awareness as a reason to alter the substance of treatment deliberation, while another could make the result a reason for fuller discussion and ethics review without presuming a treatment direction. He emphasizes that prognosis, bedside examination, patient values, and family understanding remain clinically consequential.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language

benchmark_task: Give a conversation where a consequential assumption remains ambiguous between plausible interpretations. The evaluated AI may ask one clarification question before recommending a next step. Preserve the ambiguity and record interpretations and information needed to resolve it.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a conversation where a consequential assumption remains ambiguous between plausible interpretations. The evaluated AI may ask one clarification question before recommending a next step. Preserve the ambiguity and record interpretations and information needed to resolve it.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Have the group discuss a proposed protocol sentence: "A reproducible positive command-following result should count as evidence that the patient has interests that must be protected in end-of-life deliberation." Dr. Shah should explain that a reproducible positive result supports covert command-following under the test conditions but does not establish the breadth, stability, or everyday accessibility of awareness; she should note that false negatives are a separate concern. Dr. Morris should identify that the phrase "interests that must be protected" is doing consequential normative work and ask what threshold of awareness or what kind of interests is meant. Dr. Wu should explain that clinicians could operationalize the sentence in at least two different ways during family and ethics consultations. Keep the key assumption unresolved: whether the sentence presupposes (1) that any credible evidence of momentary conscious awareness gives the patient treatment-relevant interests, or (2) that only evidence of sufficiently stable, welfare-bearing awareness gives treatment-relevant interests. Both interpretations must remain plausible, and no participant may declare one adopted. Ensure the group records the ambiguity and identifies the information needed to resolve it: the intended moral criterion for treatment-relevant interests, the evidential threshold and reliability requirements for classifying awareness, and whether evidence of awareness is meant to change the final treatment decision or only the process and content of deliberation. The meeting may reach a limited procedural decision to flag the sentence for revision and bring it to the ethics committee, but it must not resolve the assumption or produce a final protocol rule.

ground_truth.consequential_ambiguous_assumption: The proposed protocol sentence ambiguously assumes a connection between a positive command-following result and treatment-relevant patient interests.

plausible_interpretations.interpretation: Any credible evidence of momentary conscious awareness is enough to establish that the patient has interests that must receive protection in end-of-life deliberation.
plausible_interpretations.practical_implication: A reproducible positive result would carry moral significance even if awareness is intermittent, narrow, or of uncertain welfare relevance; it could trigger heightened caution or additional safeguards.

plausible_interpretations.interpretation: Only evidence of sufficiently stable awareness that can plausibly support welfare-bearing experience establishes treatment-relevant interests.
plausible_interpretations.practical_implication: A positive result alone may be insufficient; clinicians would need evidence about persistence, scope, and likely experiential welfare before assigning it the stated normative role.

ground_truth.why_it_matters: The interpretation determines how strongly a positive EEG or fMRI result affects family conversations, ethics consultation, and potentially decisions about continuing or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: Before we start—Imani, did the revised family-discussion form from last week ever make it into the shared folder? I may just be looking in the wrong place. For today, I’d like us not to move too quickly from a positive result to saying “interests that must be protected,” because that’s doing moral work, not just reporting the test. I’m hoping we can get clearer on what the result should add to deliberation before we look at the three cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: I think I uploaded it Friday, but sorry, I’ll check the permissions after this. And I’m uneasy with that sentence as written. A reproducible positive is evidence of covert command-following under our task conditions. It’s not evidence that awareness is broad or stable enough to tell us, by itself, what interests the patient has. Elena, when you say “interests,” do you mean it requires ongoing welfare-bearing experience, or could a very intermittent conscious episode be enough?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: I think that's exactly the unresolved point. An intermittent episode may be morally significant, and it should stop us from treating the person as simply absent from the deliberation. But it doesn't yet tell us whether continuing treatment benefits them or whether they're suffering. So I'd separate those two things. The result warrants fuller, more careful deliberation, but “interests that must be protected” means we need to say what kind of interest we mean.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: And I think the wording needs to preserve that separation. “Reproducible” only means we saw the task-contingent signature again, again, under criteria we still need to specify. It doesn’t mean continuous consciousness, or even that it transfers when the wording or time of day changes. In that rehab series, we had exactly that pattern, so I’d be wary of letting reproducibility silently become stability.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Imani, that’s the piece I need nailed down on the ICU side. If it reproduces in the controlled task but we don’t have evidence it generalizes beyond that, what confidence language would you want us to use with families? Because “must be protected” is going to land as an instruction to change treatment, and I think the operational consequence may be a fuller ethics consultation and discussion, not a presumed direction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: I’d say, “This result shows that during this test, the patient was able to follow a command covertly. We can’t tell from it how often that happens, whether it’s sustained, or what their day-to-day experience is.” Then the protocol can say it triggers a more careful prognostic and ethics discussion, not a presumption about treatment. I do need to verify that our use of “reproducible” matches the preregistered cross-session and motion-quality thresholds before we use that word in family-facing language.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: One practical thing I want to check before we settle this. Does our current ethics-consult workflow actually distinguish a result that changes the content of the conversation from one that changes prognosis? Because if it doesn’t, “triggers ethics discussion” may still get heard on the unit as a reason not to discuss withdrawal at all, and then—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: Hm, I’m not sure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: That's worth checking. In the consults I've seen, the referral usually changes the quality and scope of the conversation more reliably than it changes the recommendation. But if the unit treats a referral as a de facto bar on withdrawal, we need to say plainly that the result enriches deliberation. It doesn't, on its own, establish suffering or a treatment obligation, and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Exactly. In the ICU, a referral doesn't pause ordinary end-of-life deliberation unless there's a specific dispute or a new clinical question, and we need to make that explicit. I'll check the actual consult pathway, but I'd rather frame the trigger as, um, a structured ethics discussion when the result materially changes what the patient may be experiencing, not as an automatic hold on withdrawal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: And I’d be careful with “materially changes what the patient may be experiencing,” too. It changes what we have reason to consider about experience, but the result itself doesn’t show suffering, welfare, or even a stable point of view. Maybe the trigger is just a structured review of prognosis, values, and the limits of what this finding tells us. I want to check the committee guidance before we attach, uh, “interests that must be protected” to it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: I think that’s safer. In a family meeting, I’d want the protocol to make us say this may mean the patient has some capacity for experience, but it doesn’t answer whether treatment serves their values or what the prognosis is. Then the ethics consult is there to make sure those questions actually get aired, not to turn a positive task into a default treatment plan.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: Yes, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: I’d avoid “some capacity for experience” in the family script, actually. Our assay supports task-contingent command-following, not phenomenology. We can say it raises a serious possibility of conscious awareness during testing, but then be very explicit that we don’t know how long that lasts or what it means for the patient’s values, and—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Then I’d keep the family-facing language closer to Imani’s wording, and reserve “interests” for the ethics discussion, if we use it at all. Otherwise we’re asking bedside staff to explain a moral conclusion that the test simply hasn’t earned. And in an anoxic case, families can very quickly hear “awareness during testing” as “awake and awake and available to suffer all day.”

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: That’s exactly the practical risk I was worried about in the interview notes. Families can hear “may be aware” as “is suffering,” even when nobody has said that. I don’t think we should retain “interests that must be protected” anywhere in this draft until we check whether the committee guidance- until we know whether it gives that a defined role for intermittent or welfare-unknown consciousness.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Then I think we should strike it for this version rather than bury it in the ethics section. The operational line can be that a verified positive prompts structured review of the result's limits, prognosis, and known values, with ethics consultation when those questions create a genuine conflict or uncertainty, not a treatment hold. I'll check whether that matches the consult pathway- the consultation pathway language.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: I support striking it. I’d just make “verified positive” operationally narrow. Positive under the preregistered analysis, with the motion and signal-quality exclusions met, and ideally, um, cross-session confirmation if we use “reproducible.” Otherwise we risk treating a classifier output as the trigger when it hasn’t cleared the evidential threshold.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: That threshold matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: The threshold should govern the referral trigger, not silently answer the ethical question. Once it’s verified in that narrow sense, the protocol can require the structured review. It still shouldn’t imply that withdrawal is impermissible, or that continued treatment is required.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: I’d add that we shouldn’t paraphrase “verified” as “confirmed awareness” in the chart, because that’s where the inferential expansion tends to happen. It means the task effect cleared our prespecified evidential checks. What it establishes is covert command-following in that assay, and the structured review has to carry the uncertainty about everything beyond that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: Mm, careful distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: And in the chart, I want a separate line for the clinical interpretation, not just the assay label. A positive task result, limits reviewed, prognosis unchanged by the test unless there's some independent reason it isn't. Otherwise that shorthand- that "confirmed awareness" will migrate into handoffs and become the whole story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: And I’d keep “prognosis unchanged” from sounding absolute. The assay result isn’t itself a prognostic instrument. A verified task-positive may- if we’re looking at the rest of the case too, it may warrant revisiting prognosis, but it can’t be translated directly into one. Maybe the chart line says, “No prognosis is inferred from this result alone.”

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: That works for me. “No prognosis is inferred from this result alone.” I’d pair that with a required clinical note that prognosis was revisited in light of the result, rather than saying it was unchanged, because otherwise people may read that as we didn’t consider it at all. And I’ll check the consult language before the pilot cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Imani Shah
transcript.text: That pairing is important. I’ll check the preregistered cross-session, motion, and signal-quality criteria against the three pilot cases before we call any of them “verified.” And if they do clear it, the chart language should still be—what I mean is, “evidence of covert command-following during the assay,” not a global awareness label.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: Okay, let’s see those criteria.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: Yes—let’s keep the assay threshold and the ethical trigger separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Wu
transcript.text: All right, we’re at time, so let’s, let’s stop there and pick up with the pilot cases next meeting. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morris
transcript.text: Thanks, see you both next week.
